Because of different responses of tissues and selenoproteins to deﬁcient, adequate, or high levels of selenium, conclusions drawn
from measurement of one selenoprotein may not apply to all biological functions of selenium. It may be necessary to measure
several markers of functional selenium status, in particular those that apply to speciﬁc problems associated with suboptimal sele-
nium status. To cover increasing selenium concentrations resulting from a supranutritional intake selenium concentrations are most
conclusive (Bornhorst et al., 2018).
Selenium requirements and recommended dietary intakes
The requirement to prevent selenium deﬁciency is based on comparison of intakes in endemic and nonendemic Keshan disease
areas of China. However, dietary reference intakes in most countries are based on an estimate of the intake at which saturation
of plasma GPX activity occurs, obtained from studies in China and New Zealand. This estimate indicated a physiological require-
ment of approximately 45 mg day1 (Estimated Average Requirement, EAR for USA/Canada), which translated into a recommended
dietary allowance (RDA) of 55 mg day1. An increment of 5 mg day1 was added for pregnancy and 15 mg day1 for lactation. In
contrast, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommendations are lower (40 mg day1) based on the premise that full satura-
tion of GPX is unnecessary and two-thirds saturation is probably adequate (Thomson, 2004).
More recent reference values, however, consider the saturation of plasma SELENOP as adequate selenium status and were based
on additional supplementation studies measuring this biomarker (Xia et al., 2010). For example, in Australian/New Zealand and
